title: Stripe-aware eviction and NVMe QoS coordination run notes
content:
Purpose:
Run notes and early analysis for the stripe-aware eviction pilot. The goal is to test whether making eviction decisions aware of per-NVMe stripe bandwidth and active I/O can reduce tail latency and read amplification during multi-tenant KV pressure events. This doc documents experiment design, config variants, key metrics observed, and next steps.

Background/context:
- Problem: When we spill KV pages to NVMe and later rehydrate, hotty pages frequently reside across many device stripes; naive eviction/placement results in read amplification and uneven NVMe bandwidth utilization. During bursts this shows up as tail token latency spikes and sustained NVMe queue depth saturation on a subset of stripes.
- Hypothesis: If eviction prefers to keep 'stripe-coalesced' working sets (i.e., keep keys whose hot pages map to the same stripe set together) and the page reclaimer considers per-stripe queue depth and SLO headroom, we can reduce worst-case rehydration amplification and distribute read load more evenly across channels.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Baseline: current LRU-ish eviction with size-based heuristics (A).
- Variant B: Stripe-aware scoring: eviction score = recency_weight * recency + size_weight * size + stripe_fragmentation_penalty * fragmentation_score. Fragmentation_score computed from simple mapping of pgid->stripe_id counts in the residency window.
- Variant C: Stripe-Aware + NVMe-QoS feedback: same scoring as B but with an online penalty when per-stripe average latency or queue depth crosses thresholds.
- Variant D: Aggressive coalesce reclaim: attempt to evict page groups that free up contiguous stripe segments to enable sequential-ish reads on rehydration. Trade-off: higher short-term miss rate for longer-term bandwidth smoothing.
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes + one captured production replay (prod-replay-2024-09-21-small) — mixes vary tail-heavy hotkey surges and multi-tenant interleaving.

Key configuration knobs we toggled:
- fragmentation_penalty (0.0, 0.5, 1.0)
- stripe_penalty_threshold (queue_depth 16, 32)
- stripe_penalty_multiplier (1.5, 3.0)
- coalesce_group_size_limit (8 pages, 32 pages)
- nvme_probe_interval (500ms, 2s) for sampling stripe queue depths

Metrics we collected (per run):
- 95/99/99.9th token latency (ms)
- kv cache hit ratio (by page)
- nvme read amplification factor (reads performed / unique pages requested)
- per-stripe average queue depth and pct time > threshold
- background reclaim I/O bytes/sec and read op size distribution
- P50 rehydration time per-page (ms)
- application-visible error rates (timeouts, backpressure)

Summary of results (high level):
- Variant B (stripe-aware scoring) reduced nvme read amplification by ~12% on the hotkey surge synthetic workload compared to baseline, and lowered 99th token latency by ~6%. Cache hit ratio slightly decreased (~0.7%), likely due to co-location bias causing eviction of some recently-used pages in favor of preserving stripe locality.
- Variant C (QoS feedback) behaved best under mixed multi-tenant runs: observed a 20% reduction in time spent with any stripe >32 queue depth and a corresponding 10–15% drop in 99.9th token latency. The online penalty prevented overloading a single stripe during coordinated rehydrations.
- Variant D (aggressive coalesce) showed the largest drop in read op count (per-second read ops fell by ~18%) but increased average application miss latency for short bursts — i.e., P50 rehydration time rose because grouped rehydrates read more data up-front. This variant looked promising for consistent long-running bursts but worse for short spiky bursts.

Observations and profiling notes:
- NVMe device-level tracer (fio-style synthetic) confirmed that reads aligned to contiguous stripe groups had ~20% better throughput than scattered single-page reads at similar queue depths.
- In profiling the reclaim path, there was a nontrivial CPU overhead to compute fragmentation_score in C (estimated 0.8% CPU on host at 20k qps). We pushed a micro-optimization: maintain a per-resident-bucket stripe histogram incrementally to avoid scanning. With that change the overhead dropped to ~0.15% CPU.
- Background reclaim I/O volume is sensitive to coalesce_group_size_limit. Larger groups reduce op count but increase single-op sizes beyond our current read-ahead tuning which caused slightly higher per-op latency in kernel NVMe stack. Need to tune read-ahead and max_io_size in tandem.
- There are pathological cases where coalescing ties together pages from two tenants on different QoS classes; we need tenant-aware constraints to avoid QoS interference.

Representative run (prod-replay-2024-09-21-small) data excerpt:
- Baseline: P99=186ms, NVMe amp=2.9, stripe imbalance metric (max stripe qdepth / median)=5.6
- Variant B: P99=174ms, NVMe amp=2.6, stripe imbalance=3.1
- Variant C: P99=162ms, NVMe amp=2.7, stripe imbalance=1.4
- Variant D: P99=205ms, NVMe amp=2.3, stripe imbalance=1.1 (note higher P99 despite lower amp)

Failure modes and open issues:
- Metric noise: nvme read amplification calculation is sensitive to dedup/overlap accounting when prefetch hits occur. Need a canonical counter in the runtime rather than post-hoc dedupe in analysis.
- Cross-tenant fairness: without tenant labels, coalescing may preserve a single tenant's working set at the cost of others. Tagging pages with tenant id is cheap but increases metadata memory — quantify cost.
- Interaction with host-level NVMe QoS (cgroup/io.max) inconsistent across cloud providers; our stripe penalties need provider-agnostic fallback.
- Cold-start / migration: when instances are warmed from snapshots, stripe-aware heuristics sometimes mis-predict because initial stripe histograms are empty. Consider bootstrap heuristics that favor recency until histogram warm.

Concrete next steps / TODOs:
1) Implement per-bucket incremental stripe histogram as opt-in flag and benchmark CPU delta across realistic qps (owner: Ethan). Target: <0.2% CPU at 50k qps.
2) Add a canonical runtime counter for NVMe read amplification (owner: Lena) so analysis isn't reliant on logs dedupe.
3) Tenant-aware constraints: prototype with lightweight tenant tags on pages and eviction rule that avoids coalescing across QoS classes (owner: Omar).
4) Run a longer 24h mixed-tenant soak with Variant C (nvme_probe_interval=2s, stripe_penalty_multiplier=1.5) to observe steady-state fairness and degradation patterns (owner: Priya).
5) Explore pairing large coalesce_group_size_limit with increased read-ahead and kernel max_io_size adjustments in infra lab (owner: infra-eng contact TBD).
6) Draft short-run playbook for SREs describing how to toggle stripe-aware heuristics at runtime and safe rollback steps.

Notes to reviewer:
- The implementation artifacts live in GH PR: repo/PR#4123. The changes are behind runtime flags and can be gated by a config flag on host.
- I leaned conservative on penalty multipliers in early runs to avoid oscillation; we should consider an adaptive multiplier schedule in future work based on observed queue depth slope instead of absolute thresholds.
- This is a draft; please add any missing test cases you think of (esp. cross-tenant burst simulations).

Appendix (short):
- Quick pseudocode for stripe-aware eviction scoring (simplified):
  score(page) = alpha * recency_rank(page) + beta * size(page) + gamma * fragmentation(page.bucket) + (if stripe_qdepth[stripe_of(page)] > threshold then delta * penalty_multiplier else 0)
  fragmentation(bucket) = 1.0 - (most_common_stripe_count / total_pages_in_bucket)  // range 0..1

- Run IDs (for digging logs):
  run-2024-10-20-B-1
  run-2024-10-20-C-3
  run-2024-10-22-D-2

End of notes.
